Rules / Correctness

SK2034 Do not name a declaration after a reserved keyword

A declaration is named after a reserved C# keyword and can only be written with an @ escape, so every mention of it reads as a verbatim string, a typo or a keyword until the reader checks.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSyntax
Needs a compilationno
Runs under --load=looseyes
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since1.3

Why

@class, @new and @event are legal and cost the reader a stop every time. The @ on a reserved keyword is never a disambiguation the language asked for; it is the only spelling available once the name was chosen, so the finding is about the name. No fix is offered: renaming a declaration means renaming every reference, which is a refactoring rather than a text edit.

Example

Instead of:

void Register(Type @class, EventInfo @event) { }

Write:

void Register(Type declaredType, EventInfo declaredEvent) { }

The ReSharper mapping

⚠ ReSharper publishes this one as an .editorconfig key with no inspection id in its issue-type dump, and the key is resharper_escaped_keyword_highlighting, which the export sets to warning. Skala defaults the rule to suggestion, deliberately: an escaped keyword compiles and runs correctly, and the cost is entirely to the reader.

When it does not fire

⚠ Reserved keywords only, and that is what keeps the rule off load-bearing escapes. Every @ a language feature can require is on a contextual keyword — @field once field became the backing-field keyword, @value in an accessor, @extension, @record, @var, @async, @await — and a contextual keyword is a legal identifier without the escape, so an escape on one is disambiguation rather than a name to change. None of them is reported. Only the declaring identifier is reported, never a reference to it: a name that comes from another assembly must be escaped at every use site and the author cannot rename it, so reporting uses would be reporting something nobody can fix, and it would multiply one finding by its call count. Constructors and destructors are skipped because their identifier repeats the type's, which is already reported once. Namespace name parts and query continuations are not examined. Verbatim strings, interpolated verbatim strings and @ inside documentation or comments are not identifiers and are never seen.

Configuration

  • dotnet_diagnostic.SK2034.severity
